claim: The Visitor's challenge, jokes and choices are fictional editorial framing; modern comparisons concern functions, not direct invention lineages.
limit: Never present the itinerary, a purchase or the Visitor as a documented ancient event.

claim: Pompeian thermopolia sold hot food/drink using masonry counters with embedded large storage jars; Regio V preserves such a counter.
limit: No exact menu, pricing, ubiquitous kitchenlessness or modern business equivalence.

claim: A prepared-food counter offers a recognizable alternative to cooking that particular purchase yourself; jars and painted animals do not supply a complete menu.
locator: Function of thermopolium; decorated animal panels described as likely offerings.
limit: Explicit functional comparison and evidential boundary, not demographics or a recorded customer's order.

claim: The Insula del Soffitto Dipinto formed part of a Hadrianic residential/commercial block with three or four storeys and external stairs.
limit: Shown c. AD 200 with three-storey reconstructed elevation; no exact rent, owner or named residents.

claim: Its dwelling plan included a central window-lit medianum with rooms opening from it; painted decoration survives and later subdivision changed occupation.
locator: Panel paragraphs on medianum, decoration and transformation.
limit: Do not flatten all phases together or invent occupants. Scene plan is explanatory, not measured survey.

claim: Roman Bath's western range preserves tile-stack hypocaust supports; heated air circulated below floors and into walls.
limit: This bath complex, not every Roman home; occupied floor separated from furnace smoke.

claim: Vitruvius prescribes suspended hot-room floors on brick supports with a furnace; Bath's Great Bath separately received naturally hot spring water.
locator: V.10.2 and Great Bath opening paragraph.
limit: Do not apply Vitruvius's precise dimensions to Bath or confuse warm-room heating with spring temperature.

claim: Operating furnace heating involves fuel and tending; showing an unnamed attendant is a reconstruction, not a known worker's biography.
limit: No unsupported worker status, fuel quantities, wages or exact schedule.

claim: Hero's Pneumatics describes mechanical devices; first-century AD is a conventional scholarly placement, though his biography/dates are uncertain.
locator: Pneumatics sections 21/37; MacTutor chronology; Linda Hall opening.
limit: Use Roman-era Alexandria in speech; on-screen first century AD (approx.) if needed. No invention date or priority claim.

claim: Section 21 describes a coin landing on a lever plate, raising a lid/valve and allowing water to flow; when the coin falls off, the lid closes.
limit: The source says five drachms, but omit denomination. No fixed dose, coin authentication, refill automation or drink/snack vending claim.

claim: The described dispenser converts coin weight into a valve action; a reservoir still needs water and the text alone does not establish widespread installation.
locator: Section 21's finite water vessel and weight relationship.
limit: Maintenance implication and source limit are explained as such. No claim every temple used it or that it verified legal tender.

claim: Section 37 describes altar heat expanding air, moving water from a half-filled globe into a suspended bucket; descending bucket pulls chains to open doors.
limit: Illustrative small-temple model. No steam motor, electronic sensor or everyday automatic shopfront.

claim: The same design closes doors when the suspended vessel empties and a counterweight prevails; source explanations of air behaviour contain obsolete theory.
locator: Section 37 closing paragraph; MacTutor discussion of partly incorrect theory.
limit: Explain intended sequence without repeating porous-air theory or claiming a tested reconstruction. Section 38 remains separate.

claim: The five examples show recognizable functions across different places and dates; archaeological buildings and textual designs provide different kinds of evidence.
limit: Not proof that ancient life was generally easier, that modern devices directly descend from these, or that access was universal.
